zones.narrative: At 73.9°F, we're sitting right in that sweet spot where the yellowfin bite turns hot, especially with a strong temp break working the shelf—that's peak May conditions off the Hatteras shallows. I'm heading straight to the warm side of that break at 35.68N, 74.78W, where the Gulf Stream eddies are pinching baitfish against the 1400-foot drop and stacking tuna three-deep. We've got maybe two more weeks before the summer doldrums hit, so if the forecast holds, we're launching before dawn.

At 74.1°F we're sitting dead in the sweet spot, and that strong temp break is the highway—yellows will be stacked on the warm side this morning. Head straight to 36.15N, 74.73W and work the western edge of that break where the warm water peels off the Stream; watch for baitfish nervous on the color line and start chunking there. May 30th puts us at peak season, but remember the summer lull kicks in hard by mid-June, so if you're coming back next month don't expect this bite to hold.

We're sitting at 73.0°F with a hard thermal break in play—one degree shy of the sweet spot, but that strong gradient is concentrating fish on the warm side right now, so don't waste time searching cold water. Head straight to 36.70N, 74.57W and work the break itself looking for baitballs and nervous water; the warm-core eddies spinning off the Stream are stacking yellowfin this time of year. Late May is peak season, but we're already seeing the summer doldrums creep in, so if conditions don't fire by mid-morning, don't fight it—conditions can flip hard and fast out here.

With 62 degrees sitting right in that sweet spot between 58 and 65, and a strong thermal break cutting through the area, conditions are prime for a bite, but I'm launching before dawn to hit the break's cold side where the baitfish stack. I'll run straight to 37.05N, 74.71W in that 5.7-square-mile zone and start jigging the 301-foot break itself—where the shelf wall gets sharp, that's where tuna hunt. Truth is, May 30th is off-season for these waters, so don't expect the reliable winter bite; I might raise fish, but the aggressive feeding we see December through February just isn't happening yet.

At 61.1°F we're sitting right in the sweet spot and just 0.9 degrees above where the bite typically shuts down, so if that break holds strong like it is now, we've got a legitimate window before the season fully closes. We're looking at 62-degree water right on the money with a sharp temp break, which means the tuna are stacked but we're chasing them in May when they're transitioning north—they'll be scattered compared to winter's congregation. Water's sitting at 76.5°F with a strong temp break right on top of us—that's prime striker territory, only 1.5 degrees above our sweet spot and the break itself will hold bait and stack fish on the cold side. I'm heading straight to the 192-foot mark at 34.84N, 75.60W where that break sets up hardest, working the blue water edge with live bonito and watching for nervous bait balls that wahoo hunt before dawn. Fair warning though—May 30th is dead off-season for wahoo here; even with perfect conditions, these fish are thin on the grounds until July, so don't expect the October bite we live for.

We're sitting at 76.4°F with a strong temp break right in our wheelhouse—that extra 1.4 degrees above the 73–78 sweet spot means the wahoo are still keying on structure, so I'm heading out confident the break's holding bait. Start at 34.35N, 76.06W and work the cold side of that break in 152 feet, where the stack always sits inshore of the temperature wall. Real talk though—May 30th is dead season, we're two months early for the July peak, so don't expect the bite we'd get in fall; some days we'll scratch for singles.

At 76.3°F with a strong temp break sitting right at the warm edge of the wahoo sweet spot, we've got good water but we're fighting the calendar—this is off-season May, and that 34% adjusted habitat score tells me the bite will be finicky. I'd motor straight to the cold side of that break at 156 feet in the Diamond Shoals area and work the inshore lip where bait gets pinned against the structure; that's where wahoo stack when conditions align. Real talk: without chlorophyll data and with May being dead season, I'd only commit a half-day trip—full potential doesn't kick in until July.

I'll start at 94 feet where the break sharpens, staying on the warm side with my sounder ready to spot bait pods, because right now the mackerel are following threadfins and mullet through like clockwork, not hugging the thermocline. Fair warning though: it's late May, two months before the peak bite, so you'll get occasional fish but don't expect the screaming runs you'd get in August—this is scouting water, not a guarantee.
